query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating machine-learning-based interatomic potentials with an enhanced free-energy interpolation framework can yield high-fidelity estimates of fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties for both solid and liquid phases at a computational cost an order of magnitude lower than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD, even for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental and binary systems as well as multicomponent high-entropy alloys in disordered solid solutions close to melting conditions.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a hybrid computational workflow where a machine learning interatomic potential (e.g., a moment tensor potential trained on a selected subset of ab initio MD data) is used to perform efficient molecular dynamics simulations. This surrogate model is then combined with an enhanced free-energy interpolation scheme that accurately captures anharmonic vibrational contributions and electron–vibration coupling, allowing direct evaluation of free energy differences across solid and liquid phases.
generation.conditions: Simulations are performed across a temperature range spanning from below to above the fusion temperature (e.g., near-melting temperatures) in a controlled, high-temperature MD environment. The method is benchmarked under conditions typical for fusion applications, where vibrational entropy and anharmonic effects become significant.
generation.structural_mediator: The accuracy of atomic force predictions and structural correlations provided by the ML potential ensures that the underlying lattice dynamics and anharmonic vibrations are faithfully represented, mediating the computation of free-energy contributions from both ordered and disordered phases.
generation.mechanism: By training on a sparse but representative set of high-accuracy ab initio data, the ML model reproduces atomic forces and energy surfaces with near first-principles fidelity. This enables efficient sampling of the phase space and accurate interpolation of free energies, while bypassing the computational expense of continuous full ab initio MD. The enhanced free-energy interpolation explicitly retains the contributions from anharmonic effects and electron–vibration coupling.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method is predicted to reduce the computational cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio MD approaches and TOR-TILD, while matching the fidelity of free energy, vibrational entropy, and phase transition predictions over the relevant composition and temperature ranges.
generation.baseline: Conventional explicit ab initio molecular dynamics simulations and the TOR-TILD approach for elemental and binary systems.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be valid for systems where free energies of both solid and liquid phases can be adequately captured by the selected descriptors, particularly in elemental, binary, and moderately complex multicomponent high-entropy alloys. Its reliability may diminish for systems with extreme electronic complexity or where training data is sparse.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the model’s ability to capture all subtle electron–vibration interactions and rare anharmonic events in highly complex multicomponent systems; the accuracy of extrapolation beyond the training data regime remains to be rigorously established.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative elemental or binary alloy system with known ab initio free-energy curves for both solid and liquid phases near the melting temperature. First, generate a training dataset via limited ab initio MD simulations at key temperature points. Train the ML interatomic potential and employ the enhanced free-energy interpolation to compute the free energies and phase transition (fusion) temperature. Then, compare these predictions with those obtained via full ab initio molecular dynamics and with experimental benchmarks if available.
measurements: Computed free energy differences between solid and liquid phases as functions of temperature
Derived vibrational entropy values from the ML-based simulations
Predicted fusion (melting) temperature and phase transition observables
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the hybrid ML framework yields free energy curves or predicted fusion temperatures that differ from full ab initio MD/TOR-TILD results by more than the acceptable error margin (e.g., >10%) or if the method fails to capture the expected vibrational entropy trends (e.g., anharmonicity effects) across the tested temperature range.

cited_evidence.text: The extremely harsh environment of the high temperature plasma imposes strict requirements on the construction materials of the first wall in a fusion reactor. In this work, a refractory alloy system, WTaVTiZrx, with low activation and high entropy, was theoretically designed based on semi-empirical formula and produced using a laser cladding method. The effects of Zr proportions on the metallographic microstructure, phase composition, and alloy chemistry of a high-entropy alloy cladding layer were investigated using a metallographic microscope, XRD (X-ray diffraction), SEM (scanning electron microscope), and EDS (energy dispersive spectrometer), respectively. The high-entropy alloys have a single-phase BCC structure, and the cladding layers exhibit a typical dendritic microstructure feature. The evolution of microstructure and mechanical properties of the high-entropy alloys, with respect to annealing temperature, was studied to reveal the performance stability of the alloy at a high temperature. One way to achieve this would be to define a set of “good” descriptors and train a black box ML model, which can then be used to obtain properties at arbitrary compositions.
